title: The Oregon Trail
traveller: The emigrants of the Great Migration of 1843
intro: The Oregon Trail was a wagon route of 2,170 miles (3,490 km) from the Missouri River to valleys in Oregon Territory. In the Great Migration of 1843, an estimated 700 to 1,000 emigrants set out for Oregon, led at first by John Gantt, and later by Marcus Whitman.
ending: Nearly all the settlers of the 1843 wagon trains reached the Willamette Valley by early October, and a passable wagon trail now existed from the Missouri River to The Dalles. The Barlow Road, completed in 1846, made the whole way passable for wagons.

legs.title: From the Missouri to South Pass

stops.text: Independence and Westport were the main starting points on the Missouri River. Travellers leaving from Independence had to ferry across the river before following the Santa Fe Trail west.
stops.quote: the Oregon Trail's primary starting points were Independence, Missouri, or Westport

stops.text: About 200 miles (320 km) from the Missouri, the trail and nearly all its offshoots came together close to the fort along the Platte River. It was the first place on the trail to buy emergency supplies, make repairs, get medical aid or mail a letter.
stops.quote: Fort Kearny (est. 1848) is about 200 miles (320 km) from the Missouri River, and the trail and its many offshoots nearly all converged close to Fort Kearny as they followed the Platte River west.

stops.text: Travellers along the Platte passed this landmark in Nebraska, together with Courthouse and Jail Rocks, Scotts Bluff and Ash Hollow. Bison in the hundreds of thousands migrated through Nebraska on both sides of the river, and most travellers killed several for meat.
stops.quote: Notable landmarks in Nebraska include Courthouse and Jail Rocks, Chimney Rock, Scotts Bluff, and Ash Hollow with its steep descent down Windlass Hill over the South Platte.

stops.text: At the meeting of the Laramie and North Platte rivers stood a former fur trading outpost, first named Fort John, and a major stopping point. It was the last army outpost until travellers reached the coast.
stops.quote: Fort Laramie, at the confluence of the Laramie and North Platte rivers, was a major stopping point.

stops.text: The trail left the North Platte for the Sweetwater River valley, which heads almost due west, and passed this landmark on the Sweetwater. The river had to be crossed up to nine times before South Pass.
stops.quote: Independence Rock is on the Sweetwater River.

stops.text: The trail crossed the Continental Divide here. Robert Stuart's party, travelling east in 1812 and 1813, had found it as a wide and easy pass over the divide.
stops.quote: the trail crosses over the Continental Divide at South Pass, Wyoming.

legs.title: From Fort Hall to Oregon City

stops.text: Hudson's Bay Company agents told the emigrants to abandon their wagons here and use pack animals. Marcus Whitman disagreed and volunteered to lead the wagons on to Oregon.
stops.quote: When the pioneers were told at Fort Hall by agents from the Hudson's Bay Company that they should abandon their wagons there and use pack animals the rest of the way, Whitman disagreed and volunteered to lead the wagons to Oregon.

stops.text: The last crossing of the Snake River was near Old Fort Boise, made on bullboats with the stock swimming alongside. Native American boys who could swim were often hired to drive and ride the stock across.
stops.quote: The next and final crossing of the Snake River was near Old Fort Boise, and could be done on bullboats while swimming the stock across.

stops.text: The trail came to the Grande Ronde Valley near present-day La Grande, before the Blue Mountains. In 1843 settlers cut a wagon road over the mountains, which made them passable to wagons for the first time.
stops.quote: the Grande Ronde Valley near present-day La Grande before coming to the Blue Mountains. In 1843 settlers cut a wagon road over these mountains making them passable for the first time to wagons.

stops.text: The trail went to the Whitman Mission near Fort Nez Perce, where some emigrants built rafts or hired boats to go down the Columbia. After the Whitmans were killed by Native Americans in 1847, the trail bypassed the closed mission.
stops.quote: The trail went to the Whitman Mission near Fort Nez Perces in Washington until 1847 when the Whitmans were killed by Native Americans.

stops.text: The lack of a road around Mount Hood stopped the wagons. They were taken apart and floated down the Columbia River, while the animals were herded over the Lolo trail.
stops.quote: The wagons were stopped at The Dalles, Oregon, by the lack of a road around Mount Hood.

stops.text: Travellers who floated down the Columbia made a portage of 1.6 miles (2.6 km) around the Cascade Rapids before reaching the Willamette River near Oregon City, the trail's nominal end. Many settlers stopped short of it or turned off earlier.
stops.quote: The Oregon Trail's nominal termination point was Oregon City, at the time the proposed capital of the Oregon Territory.

notes: The article gives the 1843 migration's route only in outline: dated events are Fort Hall, the Blue Mountains, The Dalles and the arrival in the Willamette Valley by early October 1843. The other stops are the trail's stages from the Routes section, so their date and year are null. Fort Kearny (est. 1848) and Fort Laramie (bought by the army 1848) did not stand as army forts in 1843, so those stops describe the trail generally. The Blue Mountains are a range, so the stop is the Grande Ronde Valley at La Grande: check the point. The Oregon City stop is by 'sea' in the sense of the Columbia boats, but many travelled by the Barlow Road; the by-field is doubtful. Whitman Mission is described by the article as 'until 1847'. Left out: Salmon Falls, Three Island Crossing, Soda Springs, Fort Bridger (named with a feature but little that happened for emigrants of 1843; Salmon Falls only says Native Americans fished and traded salmon there). The article says nothing of what the emigration meant to the Native nations whose lands the trail crossed, and names no nation along the route; it only says the Great Plains were set aside by the U.S. government for Native American settlements, and that Native Americans were killed or hired. The article states Willamette Valley arrival without naming Oregon City.
